machine.cpu: 1x Intel Xeon Gold 6246R (Cascade Lake), 16 cores, 2 HWT/core
machine.memory: node 0: 192 GB DDR4  |  node 1: 730 GB Intel Optane PMEM, cpuless, KMEM DAX system-ram
machine.network: 1 GbE management only; no HPC fabric
machine.coverage_caveat: One machine, one node, and there is only one of it. Nothing here speaks to node-to-node variability, and it cannot -- this is a single lab workstation, not a partition of a large system. Its value is as a second, independently-built data point of a different vendor and a different memory technology, not as a population.
machine.tool_validation: Intel MLC v3.12 is the reference instrument here rather than a tool under test; ptrchase was originally validated against it on this machine before being taken to Frontier. The cross-tier copy matrix is a separate, independently written tool that verifies placement via move_pages before timing rather than trusting first touch.
machine.why_this_machine: Frontier and corsys4 share no vendor, no memory technology and no firmware stack. What they share is a NUMA distance table, which is the claim under test. A second machine is the only way to tell an AMD firmware defect from a property of how the SLIT is used.

mlc_matrices.note: MLC was invoked once per matrix; it averages internally over its own repetitions but does not report a spread, and the invocation was not repeated. Treat every MLC number here as n=1 at the invocation level. This is weaker provenance than the Frontier matrices (3 explicit passes) and confidence levels below are set accordingly -- the contradictions survive only because their margins are 38-69%, not because the measurement is tight.

copy_matrix.note: Single-threaded copy matrix reproduced twice within 0.5%.

ptrchase_curve.note: Cache curves run once per page size on 2026-08-06. Plateau boundaries land on declared cache sizes exactly, which is itself the check; the individual points are not replicated.

declared.l1d: 32 KB per core (512 KiB total / 16 cores)
declared.l2: 1 MB per core (16 MiB total / 16 cores)

results.margin: Every plateau boundary falls on a declared capacity: the step out of L1d is between 32K and 64K, out of L2 between 1M and 2M, out of L3 between 32M and 64M against a declared 35.75 MB. No boundary is off by a factor of two.
results.consequence: None -- this is the control. It is also the calibration check for the latency tool itself, and it passing is what licenses the page-size result below.
results.note: Same verdict as Frontier. Structure is the part machines describe reliably, and that is true on both vendors.

results.margin: The allowed mask is the full declared set. No cores are withheld.
results.consequence: None. Recorded because the same claim on Frontier is misleading -- one core per L3 group is OS-reserved there. A confirmation on one machine and a contradiction on the other is what makes the claim worth carrying in a portable registry.
results.probe_gap: The registry's probe has two halves: read the allowed mask, then attempt to exceed it. Only the first half ran. There is no batch scheduler on this machine to reject an oversubscription, so the falsifying half of the probe is not available here.
results.next_step: None available on this machine; the probe is complete only under a resource manager.

declared.detail: node 0: CPUs 0-31, 192 GB. node 1: no CPUs, 730 GB.
declared.implication: Two NUMA domains, presented by the same interface, in the same units, as peer placement targets.

results.margin: The declared count is correct and the partition is real. What fails is the peer assumption behind it: node 1 has no CPUs, so its diagonal cannot be measured at all, and reaching it costs 2.35x the latency and 0.35x the bandwidth of node 0. These are not two of the same kind of thing.
results.consequence: Anything that treats NUMA nodes as interchangeable placement units -- default first-touch under memory pressure, round-robin interleave, most NUMA-aware allocators -- will silently place hot data on persistent memory and report no error. The count is right and the model behind it is wrong.
results.note: Frontier's four domains ARE peers -- local latency, peak bandwidth and cache hierarchy are equivalent across all four, and this claim is confirmed there. The same interface, on this machine, presents a DRAM node and a persistent-memory node in identical language. The registry question is portable; the answer is not.

declared.source: ACPI SLIT via numactl -H, relayed by hwloc_distances_get
declared.implication: Reaching node 1 costs 1.70x a local access.

results.margin: The declared 1.70x understates the measured latency cost by 38% and the measured bandwidth cost by 69%. Beyond the calibration error, the two measured ratios disagree with each other by 22% -- so there is no value of the scalar that would have been right for both metrics.
results.consequence: Everything reading numa_distance() underestimates what crossing costs, and here the far node is a different memory technology, so the underestimate lands on migration and tiering policy specifically. A tiering engine that prices demotion off the declared distance is off by more than a third before it starts.
results.note: The cross-machine finding is NOT that both SLITs understate cost -- checked, and they do not. Frontier declares 1.200x for every remote hop and measures 1.063-1.182x, so its scalar is close to the right average and its failure is that it ERASES STRUCTURE: four domains declared equidistant, three tiers measured, spanning 11%. corsys4 has only two nodes so there is no structure to erase, and the failure is that the SCALAR IS SIMPLY WRONG -- 1.70x declared against 2.35x latency and 2.87x bandwidth. Two machines, two distinct failure modes, same data model. That is the stronger claim: neither is a calibration error that better firmware numbers would fix, because one scalar per pair cannot hold tiers, direction, or two metrics that disagree with each other.
results.conditions_caveat: Single MLC invocation, sequential access, so these are not directly comparable in absolute nanoseconds to Frontier's 3-pass random pointer chase. The ratios are internally consistent (same tool, same run, same conditions on both arms) and that is what the claim rests on. The tier gap is independently reproduced by the copy matrix, which verifies placement via move_pages rather than trusting first touch.

declared.implication: One scalar per pair; direction is not representable.

conditions.placement: numa_alloc_onnode, verified via move_pages before timing

results.margin: 3.46x directional asymmetry at 16 threads, against a tool reproducible to 0.5%. This is not a marginal effect; the cost of the 0<->1 pair differs by a factor of three depending on which way the bytes move.
results.consequence: No scalar distance can express this. As on Frontier, the declared model is not merely miscalibrated but structurally insufficient -- and the magnitude here makes the point unarguable.
results.note: The mechanism is that the destination tier sets the cost -- writing to Optane costs 6.4-6.7 GB/s regardless of where the data was read from, so the matrix bands vertically rather than along the diagonal. And the asymmetry INVERTS at one thread (3.63 vs 3.00), because Optane writes barely scale with threads while the read path scales well. A single directional scalar would be wrong at one thread count or the other; there is no thread-independent answer to record. Frontier's directional asymmetry is 3.9 ns against a 1.2 ns floor (3.3x noise); here it is a factor of 3.46 in the quantity itself. Same structural defect in the declared model, two orders of magnitude apart in how obvious it is.
results.conditions_caveat: The registry's probe for this claim is a directional pointer chase plus a directional bandwidth matrix, and the pointer-chase arm is UNFALSIFIABLE on this machine: node 1 has no CPUs, so no thread can be resident on it and the 1->0 direction cannot be initiated. The verdict above rests on a substitute probe -- cross-tier copy bandwidth -- which measures a read+write pair rather than a directed read. Recorded as a substitution, not as the registry's probe.

results.reason: No accelerator of any kind is installed. The claim has no referent on this machine.
No accelerator. Note this is the highest-value open claim on Frontier and it is not merely unanswered here -- it is unaskable, which is a different state and has to be recorded as one.
No accelerator, therefore no device-to-device links.

conditions.verification: tool reports the backing it actually got, per size, rather than trusting the madvise return

measured.result: hugetlb reported at every buffer size from 4 KB to 1 GB on the huge arm; 4K reported at every size on the 4K arm

results.margin: The two arms report different backing at every size, and the resulting latency curves separate. A silently-failed huge-page request would have produced identical curves.
results.consequence: None here -- but this claim passing is a precondition for cost.page_size_penalty below being a real measurement rather than a false null.
results.note: Contradicted on Frontier, where the compute-node pool is effectively empty and both normal paths to huge pages fail silently. The second control: the same claim, the same probe, opposite verdicts, and the difference is a machine configuration fact rather than a vendor defect.

results.reason: Four Ethernet interfaces exist but only one is up, and it carries management traffic. There is no HPC fabric, no multi-rail placement decision, and no MPI job spanning nodes. The claim asks how a job maps onto multiple NICs; on a single-node workstation there is no such mapping to get wrong.

regimes.reason: TLB reach covers the working set at both page sizes
first-level dTLB reach starting to fail
PEAK 1. 256 PTEs at 4K exceeds first-level dTLB reach while the data is still L2-resident (L2 is 1 MB per core).
recovered by the second-level TLB; data L3-resident
PEAK 2. 8192 PTEs at 4K exceeds second-level STLB reach while the data is still L3-resident (L3 is 35.75 MB).
both effects saturated; settles to a roughly constant offset

results.shape: Zero, then 2.72x, then partial recovery, then 1.74x, then a constant offset. Two peaks, not one.
results.consequence: TLB misses reported as memory latency, twice, at two different working-set sizes. Both peaks sit where the data is still cache-resident, which is exactly where a developer would not look for a memory-system problem.
results.note: This is the strongest cross-machine result in the pair. Frontier shows ONE peak (2.4x at 32 MiB, data L3-resident); corsys4 shows TWO (2.72x at 1 MB with data in L2, 1.74x at 32 MB with data in L3). The mechanism is identical on both machines -- the penalty peaks where TLB reach fails while the data is still cache-resident -- but the regime boundaries land at completely different sizes because the TLB and cache geometries differ. A scalar 'huge pages are ~2x better' would be wrong at nearly every size on both machines, and wrong in different places on each. This is the case for carrying curves rather than numbers, made twice.
results.conditions_caveat: The dTLB and STLB entry counts behind the mechanism are vendor specification for this microarchitecture, not measured here. The PTE counts (256 at 1 MB, 8192 at 32 MB) are arithmetic; the attribution to a specific TLB level is inference.

conditions.note: membind, NOT MLC's -j flag -- see pitfalls

results.consequence: On Optane the entire high-load region buys nothing. Injecting at delay 100 gives 98.6% of peak bandwidth at 674 ns; backing off to delay 400 gives 98.0% at 388 ns. The last 0.6% of bandwidth costs 286 ns -- 74% more latency for six-tenths of one percent of throughput. A tiering engine that saturates the persistent-memory tier is paying that for nothing.
results.note: The two tiers have different curve SHAPES, not just different offsets. DDR4 trades 7.5% of bandwidth for 1.52x latency; Optane trades 2.0% for 1.37x and is bandwidth-saturated so early that the first third of the sweep is flat. Frontier's DDR4 knee is more generous than either (98.3% of peak at 3.6x lower latency), so the shape is not even a property of the memory technology alone.
results.conditions_caveat: Read-only traffic. The 1:1 read-write mix is where Optane's real cost lives -- 5.5 GB/s against 97.4 GB/s for DDR4, an 17.8x gap versus the 2.9x read-only gap. Any conclusion drawn from this curve applies to read-dominated phases only.

results.reason: No accelerator, so there is no host-to-device transfer to price. Recorded rather than omitted because this machine HAS the analogous cost -- cross-tier DRAM<->Optane copy -- and the registry has no claim for it. See open_questions: the second machine found a gap in the portable question list, which is the portability test doing its job.

results.next_step: Re-run the cross-tier copy matrix under a controlled background load, with the load generator pinned off the copying threads so core pressure and bandwidth pressure are separable. The Frontier attempt at this claim was confounded for exactly that reason; the fix is known and untried here.

flagged.statement: Cross-tier copy asymmetry inverts with thread count. At 16 threads promotion (Optane->DRAM, 23.21 GB/s) is 3.46x cheaper than demotion (DRAM->Optane, 6.71 GB/s). At one thread it reverses: promotion 3.00 GB/s is SLOWER than demotion 3.63 GB/s. Optane writes scale 1.9x from 1 to 16 threads; the promotion path scales 7.8x.
flagged.promotion_criteria: A thread sweep (1, 2, 4, 8, 16) on both directions, which would locate the crossover and show whether the scaling is smooth or has a knee of its own.
flagged.if_true_would_predict: A single-threaded migration engine lands on the wrong side of the asymmetry it is designed to exploit.
flagged.why_flagged: Both arms are real measurements reproduced within 0.5%, so the observation itself is solid. What is flagged is the generalisation -- two thread counts is not a scaling curve, and the crossover point between them is unmeasured. 'Promotion is cheap' is being asserted as a multi-threaded property on the basis of two samples.

pitfalls.symptom: MLC reports Optane at ~106 GB/s and ~76 ns -- marginally faster than DRAM, which is physically impossible.
pitfalls.cause: MLC's -j<n> flag places memory by running the initialising thread on a CPU of node n and relying on first touch. Node 1 has no CPUs. It does not warn and does not fail; it allocates from node 0 and reports DRAM numbers under an Optane label.
pitfalls.remedy: Use numactl --membind=<n>, which constrains the page allocator directly and needs no CPU on the target node. Sanity check for any node-1 run: read bandwidth must land near 32 GB/s, never near 106 GB/s.
pitfalls.sting: This is the canonical unsuitable-probe failure: the instrument's own placement mechanism silently degrades to the thing you are trying to measure against. It is the same class of error as verifying GPU affinity with a bandwidth probe on Frontier.

pitfalls.symptom: A loaded-latency curve plotted from these files zigzags instead of forming a clean L.
pitfalls.cause: Points ordered by bandwidth rather than by inject delay. Near saturation many delays give nearly the same bandwidth at very different latencies.

pitfalls.symptom: MLC returns quietly less accurate numbers.
pitfalls.cause: MLC disables hardware prefetchers via MSR and needs root to do it. Without root it falls back silently.
pitfalls.remedy: Run as root; confirm the prefetcher line in the output header.

open_questions: The registry has no claim for cross-tier copy cost. On Frontier that cost appears as cost.host_device_transfer; here the same physical question -- what does it cost to move a page from one memory technology to another, and is it directional -- has no home, so the machine's single most useful measurement (the copy matrix) is carried under numa.symmetry as a substitute probe. A cost.tier_transfer claim would cover both machines and would make Frontier's HBM/DDR pair askable too. This is the second machine changing the portable question list, which is what a second machine is for.

Does the SLIT understate crossing cost on a third machine? Two vendors agree so far, both in the same direction. A machine where the SLIT is accurate would be the most informative single data point available, and would say the error is a choice rather than a norm.
Node 1 has no CPUs, so no CPU-initiated probe can measure direction out of it. corsys4 has DSA; a DMA-initiated transfer could measure directed cost without a resident thread. Untried.

Loaded latency is read-only here and on Frontier. Optane's read-write gap is 17.8x against 2.9x read-only, so the read-only curve is the least representative measurement in this file for anything that writes.

Is the two-peak page-size penalty a property of two TLB levels generally, or of this specific cache/TLB geometry? Frontier shows one peak. A third machine decides whether the count of peaks is predictable from the declared geometry, which would make it derivable rather than requiring measurement.
